summary: Tuftonboro (Carroll Co.), NH wood tower dedicated 1924 by Melvin Village residents; sources say it was never a fire tower; listed standing, free public access.

access.note: Free public access according to the historical marker; small trailhead parking lot on NH Route 109

visit.trail_note: Short, wide trail from a small parking lot by a gate; about five minutes to the tower (2018 visit)

events.note: Idea for the tower begun on a walk by Joshua Litchfield and Frank Speare on Edgerly Hill (per The Laker, 2018)
Dedicated in 1924 per the marker, which gives no construction date; built by residents of Melvin Village
Taller tower rebuilt 1977-78 (construction began 1977; Bill Cornell designed it; Kirk Titus hired to rebuild); re-dedicated July 22, 1978, per The Laker (2018)

notes_for_editor: The sources say the Abenaki Tower was never a fire tower, but the Forest Fire Lookout Association list classes it as an observation tower ('Obs Tower'). The editor should decide whether a fire-lookout directory should carry it; the brief's kind 'tower' does not claim fire use. The marker names the builder only as 'residents of Melvin Village'. The Laker article (2018) was read in full on the 2026-10-09 check. It names Tuftonboro resident Lewis McIntire as the winning $400 bidder to construct the tower, and describes a taller rebuild in 1977-78 (Kirk Titus hired to rebuild, Bill Cornell designed it, re-dedicated 22 July 1978). The 1977-78 rebuild is now a 'rebuilt' event and the story says so. The story keeps the marker's builder wording and does not name McIntire; the editor may decide whether the builder line needs the Laker's account. The marker page (HMDB) was read in full: its trailhead location, its 'historical and continuing contributions' wording and its Abenaki Tower Trail Association excerpt are confirmed. The association's own site was not read; it is the likeliest source for upkeep and current climbing rules. Other search snippets say the tower was 'originally constructed in 1924 by local volunteers' and describe it as stone and wood; they were not read, so they are not used. The FFLA row has no NHLR or FFLOS number. Its coordinates match the brief (43.67226, -71.29064). The climbable flag rests on the 2018 visit. About seven page reads were used for this tower, which is over the budget.
